status: Author approved immediate publication of all thirty on October 25, using October 24 article dates.
editorial_voice: Short sentences, familiar words, a natural voice, and explanations of necessary terms. Easy for non-native English readers. No invented personal incidents or deliberate grammar errors.
example_policy: Every executable example is Rust. SQL is embedded in Rust query calls. Pin engine and client versions and verify through existing GitHub CI.
selection: Established SQL engines anchor the series. DuckDB supplies the analytical strand. This is an editorial selection, not a guarantee of future market share.

articles.title: PostgreSQL from Rust: Make Related Writes Commit Together
articles.rust_example: SQLx service with bound queries, transactions, constraints, and connection limits.
verification_limits: Fixed demonstration accounts and integer credits; not a payment system or full idempotent endpoint.
Pool cap is per pool, not a fleet-wide capacity limit.
Does not cover authorization, crash recovery, or opposite-order transfer deadlocks.

articles.title: MySQL From Rust: Keep the Stock Change and Order Together
articles.rust_example: SQLx service using InnoDB tables, checked writes, and explicit commits.
verification_limits: Assertions are intended CI checks; no local engine execution. Sequential fixture does not establish concurrent throughput, ambiguous commit recovery or a complete idempotency protocol.

articles.title: SQLite from Rust: Save Local Data Without a Database Server
articles.rust_example: rusqlite app that stores local records and reopens them after restart.
verification_limits: Connection close/reopen is not an OS restart or power-loss test.
First insert ID one follows the new empty fixture; production code should obtain the inserted ID.
No backup implementation, encryption, file-permission enforcement, or cross-machine sharing.

verification_limits: No local engine execution. Contract covers selected CRUD/type/constraint behavior, not complete SQL, replication, backup, migration or performance compatibility.

articles.title: Why Two PostgreSQL Reads in Rust Can See Different Row Versions
articles.rust_example: Two SQLx connections coordinate reads and writes to expose snapshot boundaries.
verification_limits: Ordinary primary-database reads only; not caches, replicas, or every locking clause.
Stable snapshots are not a complete read-then-write business invariant.
Uses PostgreSQL 18 semantics and a tiny controlled table; no performance claim.

articles.title: Retry the Whole PostgreSQL Transaction from Rust
articles.rust_example: A bounded serialization-conflict case retries the full transaction and checks the final invariant.
verification_limits: The first-attempt intervention is test harness coordination, not production retry behavior.
Retries only received SQLSTATE 40001; not an unknown commit result or arbitrary network error.
No external effects, complete outbox, adaptive backoff, or contention benchmark.

articles.title: PostgreSQL HOT Updates: Check When a Rust Write Avoids New Index Entries
articles.rust_example: Compare controlled indexed and non-indexed updates from Rust, with server observations.
verification_limits: Current-transaction view avoids cumulative-stat flush/snapshot lag; does not claim cumulative counters update synchronously.
One small row, ample page room, B-tree indexes, fillfactor50; not a production HOT ratio.
No timing, WAL-byte, vacuum, table-size, or overall index-benefit measurements.

articles.title: Test PostgreSQL Row Security with a Separate Rust Application Role
articles.rust_example: Exercise separate non-owner database roles and transaction-scoped tenant context through SQLx.
verification_limits: Trusted application selects tenant context; hostile SQL under that role can set the custom context.
Owner bypass is deliberately visible; FORCE does not constrain superusers/BYPASSRLS.
One app connection makes reuse visible; not complete authorization for functions/views/admin paths.

articles.title: Recover Pending Rust Jobs After a PostgreSQL Listener Reconnects
articles.rust_example: Disconnect a Rust listener and recover work from a durable table rather than notification history.
verification_limits: Dropping/recreating a listener object is a controlled absence, not every physical network-failure mode.
One consumer, no atomic multiworker claim or crash-safe external effect.
100ms absence window is a bounded fixture wait, not a production latency measurement.

articles.title: Add a PostgreSQL Enum Value Without Surprising Old Rust Readers
articles.rust_example: Keep the old decoder in a Rust fixture while migrating the schema and introducing a new value.
verification_limits: Manual text-to-Rust decoder, not SQLx derive implementation or real released binary.
Does not implement fleet rollout gates or a compatibility presenter.
No simplistic down-migration promise; committed new-state data remains after disabling a writer.

articles.title: Your MySQL Primary Key Travels Into the Other Indexes
articles.rust_example: A Rust fixture compares schema and plan observations for two primary-key designs.
verification_limits: No local execution or performance measurement. Tiny fixture checks query semantics and prints plans/allocation; it cannot quantify production storage, fragmentation or latency.

articles.title: Reproduce a MySQL Deadlock From Rust, Then Fix the Lock Order
articles.rust_example: Coordinate opposite lock orders with two Rust tasks, then check ordered locking and bounded retries.
verification_limits: No local execution. Two-row coordinated reproduction does not establish absence of deadlocks in other plans, indexes, foreign keys or deployed traffic.

articles.title: Why a MySQL Range Read Can Block an Insert Into an Empty Gap
articles.rust_example: Use two Rust connections to observe an indexed range lock under a specified isolation level.
verification_limits: No local execution. Explicit indexed locking-read fixture excludes foreign-key/duplicate-check cases and is not a recommendation to change production isolation globally.

articles.title: Rust Says the Names Differ. MySQL Rejects the Duplicate.
articles.rust_example: Bind Unicode strings from Rust and check equality and unique constraints under explicit collations.
verification_limits: No local execution. Tests selected accent and Unicode byte cases, not complete normalization, confusable detection or a recommended universal identity policy.

articles.title: SQLite WAL Still Allows Only One Writer: Handle Busy Results in Rust
articles.rust_example: Two rusqlite connections expose writer contention and bounded busy handling.
verification_limits: Local temporary WAL file; no network filesystem or load benchmark.
Finite busy timeout is a failure bound, not a precise elapsed-time assertion or universal tuning value.
Does not implement a general retry framework or transaction-coupled external effects.

articles.title: Run rusqlite on a Worker Thread with a Bounded Tokio Queue
articles.rust_example: Move rusqlite work to a bounded database worker and check that unrelated Rust tasks can progress.
verification_limits: Readiness signal precedes SQLite execute; proves async progress while database request is pending, not a trace of the exact driver wait-start instant.
One thread/two-slot queue with fixed small jobs; not a payload-byte budget or throughput result.
Dropping reply/caller timeout does not cancel started SQLite work; no complete shutdown/cancellation framework.

articles.title: Enable SQLite Foreign Keys on Every Rust Connection
articles.rust_example: Check foreign-key enforcement on each opened connection and test deletion behavior.
verification_limits: Does not repair old orphans automatically or authorize a user's project.
No arbitrary external writer initialization guarantee or large-cascade performance test.
After initial CI, fallible foreign_key_check iteration was changed to collect Result<Vec<_>> before counting; final CI must include that correction.
